strengths: First systematic investigation of Video LLM safety; addresses critical understudied gap with strong motivation
Comprehensive VideoSafetyBench dataset (77.6k samples, 19 subcategories, 10 languages) grounded in real-world policies—valuable community resource
Clear empirical findings demonstrating 42.3% safety degradation with video modality and 65.1% improvement with VideoSafety-R1
Extensive evaluation across 14 model variants and multiple benchmarks with thorough ablation studies and cross-dataset generalization
Well-motivated dual-stage approach combining explicit harm detection (alarm tokens) with reasoning-enhanced defense (Safety-Guided GRPO)
Excellent documentation including annotation pipelines, prompts, hyperparameters, and dataset statistics supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Alarm tokens are simple learnable embeddings; GRPO and multi-task learning are established techniques. Primary contribution is application rather than methodology.

Evaluation methodology heavily relies on LLM-based assessment (Qwen-Long) with small human validation set (114 samples for 11.4k test set); unclear if single-model validation captures systematic biases
Concerning increase in False Refusal Rate from 0.7% to 13.4% (12.7% absolute increase); insufficient discussion of safety-usability tradeoff and deployment implications
VideoSafety-R1 only trained and evaluated on VideoLLaMA3-2B; generalization to other architectures, model scales, or video LLMs unclear despite indirect image-benchmark evidence
Synthetic training data (LLM-generated CoT annotations with templates) lacks comparison to human-written examples; risk of learning template artifacts rather than generalizable reasoning
Dataset construction relies on proprietary APIs for annotation (Qwen-Max-VL, VideoLLaMA3) without inter-annotator agreement metrics; 15-second clips may lose contextual information
Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; unclear stability across random seeds
Limited analysis of failure modes, category-specific underperformance (e.g., Alcohol/Tobacco), or sophistication of semantic attacks explored
No comparison with alternative safety alignment approaches (Constitutional AI, DPO variants, other fine-tuning strategies) beyond base LLM baseline
Proprietary dependencies (Qwen models, GPT-4o for annotation; Qwen-Long for evaluation) limit full reproducibility despite code availability claims
